content.text:
What Kind of Story Is The North Wind and the Sun?

The North Wind and the Sun is an Aesop fable in which the two, arguing over who is stronger, hold a contest to see which can make a traveler take off his coat. It carries a short but deep lesson: warmth moves the heart more than sheer force.

content.alt: The North Wind and the Sun - The original story
content.text:
The Original Story

This is a fable from Aesop of ancient Greece, some 2,600 years ago (international folktale type ATU 298). The North Wind fails to blow off the traveler's coat with a fierce gale, while the Sun's warm rays lead the traveler to take it off himself — an ending that captures the lesson, "persuasion is stronger than force."

content.alt: The North Wind and the Sun - Plot summary
content.text:
Plot Summary

Under a clear sky, the North Wind and the Sun argue over who is stronger, and agree that whoever can first get the traveler's coat off will win. The harder the North Wind blows its cold gusts, the tighter the traveler wraps his coat around him. Then the Sun sends down warm rays, and the traveler takes off his coat himself in the heat — so the Sun wins.
content.caption: The triumph of warmth

content.alt: The North Wind and the Sun - The lesson it teaches
content.text:
The Lessons of The North Wind and the Sun

The heart of it is that hearts are moved when we approach with warmth rather than force. Talk it over with your child: "When a friend won't listen to you, what could you do?"
content.caption: The warmth that opens hearts

content.alt: The North Wind and the Sun - How to read it aloud
content.text:
How to Read It Aloud

Change your voice — make the North Wind rough and forceful, and the Sun soft and easygoing. Make the "whoooosh!" of the wind together, and point out how force can backfire with "Why did the traveler bundle up tighter the more the wind blew?" Best suited for ages 3 to 6.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. What age is The North Wind and the Sun good for?
A. It suits ages 3 to 6. With simple characters and a clear lesson, it makes a great first fable.

Q. What is the lesson?
A. "Warmth is stronger than force." The message is that what moves people is not power but kindness.

Q. What kinds of conversations are good to have?
A. Talk together about "pushing versus speaking warmly" and "a moment when your own heart was moved."
